text: Protecting U.S. workers and preventing abuse of the H-1B program are legitimate policy goals. However, the proposed uniform $103,265 fee is not supported by a sufficiently complete economic analysis and should not be finalized as written. The demand analysis in Sections VI.A.3 and VI.A.4 focuses primarily on employers and workers already participating in the H-1B process. It does not adequately consider choices made years before a petition is filed. International students decide where to study, skilled professionals decide where to build their careers, and companies decide where to locate teams well in advance. Continued short-term demand for 85,000 visas therefore would not establish that the fee has little economic effect. A smaller pool of students and professionals choosing the United States would reduce the country's opportunities to attract the relatively small number of people who may later create companies, develop important technologies, or make other exceptional contributions. Employers may also respond by locating additional work outside the United States. These effects are central to the proposal, but Table 12 lists the effects on wages and economic growth as "N/A." Before finalizing the rule, DHS should evaluate its likely effects on international-student enrollment, retention of U.S.-educated graduates, innovation, entrepreneurship, startup survival, offshoring, team location, tax revenue, and employment of complementary U.S. workers. The research supporting the demand estimate also requires further examination. The NPRM cites the February 2026 version of George Borjas's working paper, while the currently available paper was materially revised in August 2026. Research by Michael Clemens disputes several assumptions underlying the earlier estimate, including the comparison years, definition of local labor markets, employer tenure, and comparison of H-1B base salary with total wage income for U.S. workers. DHS should identify the exact version on which it relied, address the conflicting evidence, and publish sensitivity analyses showing how its conclusions change under different assumptions about wages, tenure, productivity, turnover, offshoring, and long-term participation. Current excess registrations do not prove that demand will remain unchanged after students, workers, employers, and business units adjust their decisions. The ability-to-pay analysis in Section III.B is also unpersuasive. DHS compares the fee with six years of gross wages. Wages are an employer expense, not profit or available cash. The fee would be due up front, even though a petition may be denied and the employee may not remain with the employer for six years. Six years of payroll is therefore not a reliable measure of an employer's ability to absorb a $103,265 charge. The proposal would also favor large incumbent companies over startups and smaller employers. DHS estimates that 11,051 small entities—76 percent of the affected small entities it identified—would incur costs exceeding one percent of revenue. A uniform fee could prevent smaller companies from competing for specialized talent even when their need is legitimate. DHS should evaluate less harmful alternatives, including a graduated fee based on employer size, with aggregation rules for affiliated companies to prevent avoidance; reduced fees for graduates of U.S. institutions; and objective, auditable exceptions for unusually experienced or specialized professionals. Concerns about displacement and abuse can be addressed more directly through prevailing-wage enforcement, penalties for repeat violators, oversight of third-party placements, and stronger worker portability. These measures target employer conduct rather than imposing the same charge on every cap-subject petition. For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed uniform fee or substantially revise it after completing a fuller economic analysis. Protecting U.S. workers and attracting global talent are not conflicting objectives. A targeted system can pursue both, while a uniform six-figure fee risks shrinking the future talent pool, encouraging offshoring, and concentrating access to skilled workers among the largest employers.

text: I strongly support the proposed fee and urge DHS to finalize it. The H-1B program as it operates today is not a talent program it is a wage-arbitrage scheme that has displaced American workers. Congress created the H-1B category for specialty occupations that could not be filled domestically. The program's own records show it has become something else entirely. USCIS's Characteristics reports for FY 2023 through 2025 show that computer-related occupations account for 62 to 65 percent of approved petitions, that custom computer programming services is the single largest industry sector at roughly a quarter of all petitions, and that about 70 percent of beneficiaries are born in one country, with no other country outside the top two exceeding 2 percent. No honest reading of these numbers supports the claim that the program surveys the world for the best talent in every field. It is a pipeline, built and operated by outsourcing firms, that delivers mid-level programmers into American companies at below-market rates. The statutory wage floor is also fiction. INA §212(n)(1)(A) requires employers to attest to paying the higher of the actual or prevailing wage. That sounds protective. In practice, the Department of Labor's Level I prevailing wage sits near the 17th percentile of local wages and Level II near the 34th, so an employer can satisfy the statute while paying a third less than the median worker in the same job and city. DHS's own analysis in the weighted-selection rulemaking found that 28 percent of cap petitions from FY 2020 through 2024 were filed at Level I and 55 percent at Level II. Eighty-three percent of the program is below-median labor by design. The program's defenders say it brings the world's best talent to the United States. Nothing in its design has ever selected for that. The talent argument is also false. The United States already has visa categories built specifically for exceptional individuals. If a candidate is truly among the best in the world, those pathways exist, and a fee on H-1B would not stand in the way. The workers who would be priced out by this fee are, by definition, the ones whose employers value them at less than the fee. That is not the population the "best and brightest" argument describes. If H-1B beneficiaries were the scarce, elite talent industry claims, employers would already be paying them accordingly and the fee would be a rounding error. The intensity of opposition to the fee is itself proof that much of the program's value to petitioners comes from paying less, not from hiring the exceptional. The fee is also justified on cost grounds. The H-1B program is not run by USCIS alone, and its actual cost has never been charged to the employers who profit from it. A single petition spans multiple agencies. The Department of Labor sets wages and investigates violations, the Department of State vets applicants abroad, USCIS investigates fraud, and the Department of Justice litigates discrimination against U.S. workers. Transitioning a worker to a green card adds PERM certification and further visa processing. This is a massive workload funded by taxpayers or by outdated fees. Fraud adds a heavy enforcement burden. Shell companies, fake degrees, lottery manipulation, and unpaid benching require site visits, investigations, and litigation across federal entities, including USCIS, DOL, DOJ, and ICE as a few examples of agencies. Yet, employers currently pay fees measured only in the low thousands. A $103,265 fee is not a penalty it is an initial attempt to match the program's true administrative costs. When a program demands extensive multi-agency policing and continuously generates fraud and discrimination, it should fully fund its own oversight. Employers objecting to the price are simply refusing to pay for the regulation their own conduct made necessary.

text: I oppose this proposed $103,265 fee on H-1B cap-subject petitions. It goes beyond what DHS is legally allowed to do on its own, isn't backed by numbers that hold together, and will push skilled workers and employers out of the U.S. instead of protecting the system it claims to fund. 1. This Is a Tax, Not a Fee DHS can only charge fees under INA §286(m) for services it actually provides. But only 34.2% of this fee goes to USCIS, the agency that processes H-1B petitions. The rest funds DOJ immigration courts (33.7%), ICE (11.9%), DOL (13.8%), and DOS/CBP (6.4%) - agencies that provide no service to the filer at all. A charge not tied to a specific service to the payer is legally a tax, and only Congress can impose taxes (Nat'l Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 1974). DHS's own proposal admits it has "never" done this before. 2. This Is Congress's Call, Not an Agency's Congress set the H-1B caps, the wage rules, and the existing fees. This charge is almost identical to the $100,000 Proclamation 10973 fee already struck down in court (California v. Mullin, on appeal). Passing a near-identical fee through rulemaking while that case is pending looks like an end-run around the courts. And at $8.8 billion a year, this is exactly the kind of major decision the "major questions doctrine" says needs clear approval from Congress, not an old cost-recovery clause (West Virginia v. EPA, 2022). 3. The $8.8 Billion Number Doesn't Add Up: DHS assumes 85,000 petitions get filed every year, while its own report predicts employers will hire less because of this exact fee, and finds 76% of small sponsoring employers would be significantly harmed. DHS can't claim the fee will scare off filers and also assume filing volume won't drop. Courts call this "arbitrary and capricious" (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 1983). 4. This Group Already Pays Into the System: International students pay 2-3 times what citizens pay in tuition, with no federal aid. Once working on OPT or H-1B, they pay full federal, state, and payroll taxes, often without ever collecting Social Security or Medicare. A $103,265 fee on top of that isn't cost recovery. It's a second tax on people who have no vote and no lobby. 5. This Drives Talent Away, It Doesn't Raise Money If sponsorship gets this expensive, the talent doesn't vanish - it goes to Canada, the UK, the EU, or Australia. Many major U.S. companies today were founded or are led by people who came here as international students through this same path. 6. The Number Isn't Based on Any Real Cost $103,265 wasn't calculated from what it actually costs to process a petition. It was reached by dividing a revenue target ($8.78 billion) by an assumed number of filings (85,000). A number worked backward from a revenue goal is a tax, not a fee. 7. DHS Never Analyzed the Fees Stacking Together DHS admits that if the vacated $100,000 Proclamation fee comes back on appeal, employers could owe both fees - over $200,000 per petition. The rule includes no analysis of what that combined cost would mean, even though DHS knows it's a real possibility. For these reasons, I ask DHS to withdraw this fee. At the very least, it should be scaled back to what USCIS actually spends adjudicating an H-1B petition, since that's what §286(m) allows. The pieces meant to fund ICE, CBP, EOIR, DOS, and DOL don't belong here at all, that kind of spending needs Congress, not a fee rule. DHS should also redo the revenue numbers honestly, accounting for the drop in filings this fee will itself cause and the chance it stacks with the Proclamation fee. And if DHS moves ahead regardless, small businesses, startups, hospitals, and research institutions shouldn't be priced out entirely without some kind of relief. Respectfully commenting

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16965

text: I oppose rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and urge the Forest Service to retain its core protections. I live in the Southeast, where I think the value of protecting remaining roadless National Forest lands is especially easy to see. Our National Forests are not enormous expanses of undeveloped federal land surrounded by more wilderness. They are often islands of relatively intact forest within a region that is heavily developed, privately owned, and crossed by roads. In the Southern Appalachians in particular, roadless areas protect some of the most biologically diverse forests in the country. They also protect steep mountain slopes, headwater streams, cold-water fisheries, and watersheds that ultimately provide clean water to communities downstream. Building additional permanent roads through these areas creates impacts that extend well beyond the footprint of the road itself, including erosion, sedimentation, habitat fragmentation, invasive species access, and long-term maintenance obligations. As someone who lives in this region, I also value these lands for recreation. The ability to hike, camp, hunt, fish, and explore large areas of public forest that have not been divided by an extensive road network is increasingly unusual in the Southeast. National Forest roadless areas provide something that state parks, suburban greenways, and smaller recreation areas simply cannot replace. I understand the Forest Service’s argument that managers need flexibility to address wildfire, hazardous fuels, insects, disease, and forest restoration. I support active management where it is actually necessary. But I do not believe those needs justify eliminating a nationwide conservation rule. This distinction is particularly important in the Southeast. Our forests, climate, fire ecology, terrain, and development patterns are not identical to those of the western United States. A national policy change justified substantially by concerns about catastrophic wildfire and forest-management constraints should not unnecessarily expose Southern Appalachian roadless lands to permanent road construction and development. Where intervention in a roadless area is genuinely necessary for public safety, ecological restoration, prescribed fire, or wildfire mitigation, the Forest Service should have carefully tailored mechanisms for doing that. Those situations should be addressed directly rather than used as justification for removing protection from roadless areas generally. I am particularly concerned about permanent road construction primarily intended to make commercial timber extraction or other development economically feasible. That is fundamentally different from allowing a land manager to conduct a necessary prescribed burn, restore an ecosystem, or protect a community from wildfire. For the Southeast, preserving roadless areas means protecting intact Appalachian forests, clean headwaters, wildlife habitat, trout streams, steep slopes, and increasingly scarce opportunities for genuine backcountry recreation. These are long-term public assets. Once a road is built and an intact area is fragmented, recreating what was lost is extremely difficult. I therefore urge the Forest Service to retain the 2001 Roadless Rule or adopt a narrower alternative that preserves its conservation baseline while allowing carefully defined exceptions for demonstrated forest-health, restoration, and public-safety needs. We do not need to choose between responsible forest management and protecting our remaining roadless public lands. The Forest Service should pursue both.

text: I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a new $103,265 fee on all cap-subject H-1B petitions, codified at 8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(xii). This fee should be withdrawn in its entirety. It is arbitrary in its derivation, unlawful in its underlying rationale, and destructive in its economic effect. 1. The fee is not a fee — it is an unlawful tax in disguise Agency fee authority under INA §286(j) and (m) exists to recover the actual costs of adjudicating and administering a specific benefit. DHS’s own methodology disproves any claim to that standard: the agency began with a total revenue target of $8,777,488,035, divided it by an assumed volume of 85,000 petitions, and arrived at $103,264.57 — rounded to $103,265. This is reverse-engineered budget allocation, not cost recovery. A charge that starts from “how much money do we want” rather than “what does this task cost” is a tax, and DHS has no statutory authority to levy one. A federal court already struck down the administration’s prior $100,000 H-1B fee on precisely this ground in June 2026 (Judge Sorokin, D. Mass.), holding that only Congress may impose taxes on visa applications. Restructuring the identical outcome through notice-and-comment rulemaking does not cure the underlying constitutional defect — it only changes the procedural vehicle. 2. The revenue allocation confirms this is general taxation, not program funding DHS’s own table shows the money is not even being used to adjudicate H-1B petitions. Only 34.2% goes to USCIS. The remainder is diverted to EOIR (33.7%), DOL (13.8%), ICE (11.9%), DOS (5.5%), and CBP (0.9%) — agencies with no role in adjudicating the H-1B petition the fee is nominally attached to. 3. The fee is economically indefensible and disproportionately harms small business DHS’s own regulatory impact analysis concedes the rule would have a significant economic impact on 11,051 small entities — 76% of all small businesses that filed cap-subject petitions in FY2025 — and states plainly that it identified no alternative that would reduce that burden. This is not a marginal side effect; it is the agency acknowledging it is knowingly imposing a potentially existential cost on thousands of small employers, hospitals, engineering firms, and startups that rely on specialized talent they cannot otherwise source domestically, with no mitigation contemplated. A fee of this size — over 100 times the current base filing fee — does not merely discourage marginal or abusive filings. It functions as a blanket exclusion. Small businesses, regional hospitals, university-adjacent research firms outside the cap-exempt category, and startups will simply be unable to compete with large corporations that can absorb six-figure fees per hire. This fee does not target fraud or misuse; it targets company size and access to capital, handing an enormous structural advantage to the largest incumbents in every industry that uses the program. 4. Stacking fees compounds the harm without justification DHS confirms this fee is layered on top of the base I-129 fee, the ACWIA fee, the fraud prevention and detection fee, the Asylum Program Fee, fees under the April 2026 interim final rule, premium processing, and any reinstated proclamation-based payment — with DHS stating explicitly that an employer subject to multiple charges must pay all of them cumulatively. No cost-based justification is offered for why H-1B petitioners alone should shoulder cumulative six-figure charges when no comparable multiplier applies to other employment-based petition categories. 5. The rule undermines, rather than serves, the government’s own economic interests The H-1B program fills documented shortages in specialty occupations — engineering, healthcare, IT, and advanced sciences — where domestic labor supply is insufficient. A fee at this level will not improve adjudication quality or program integrity; it will suppress legitimate hiring, push economic activity and jobs to competitor nations with more rational immigration-cost structures, and reduce the very tax and payroll revenue the government collects from these positions and the U.S. workers who work alongside them. DHS has not offered any analysis showing the projected $8.8 billion in fee revenue exceeds the broader economic activity, tax revenue, and domestic job creation this rule would suppress. Conclusion For the reasons above, I respectfully but firmly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety. If the Department believes additional cost recovery is warranted, any future proposal should be (1) tied transparently to the actual, itemized cost of adjudicating H-1B petitions, (2) limited to funding the agency actually performing that adjudication, and (3) subject to a genuine small-business impact mitigation analysis, rather than an acknowledgment of harm with no remedy offered.

text: I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $103,265 fee on all H-1B cap-subject petitions. It rests on an unsound economic justification and would fall as a blunt, across-the-board barrier on a highly specialized, graduate-educated workforce. 1. The economic case is unsound. DHS relies on Borjas (2026) to claim employers would pay $100k to $200k and demand will not fall below 85,000 (91 FR 54835). But a single paper estimating a maximum willingness to pay does not show that setting the fee at that ceiling is harmless. It implies the fee captures nearly the entire surplus of an H-1B hire, driving out smaller and lower-margin employers. DHS's own data confirms harm: it projects volume falling about 12% (from 96,750 to 85,000; Table 13) and concedes a significant impact on 11,051 small entities, 76% of small filers (91 FR 54836 to 54837), while offering no exemption. Its "inelastic demand" finding is extrapolated from fee changes a fraction of this size; a 100-to-1,000 times jump is unsupported. 2. The fee hits a graduate-educated workforce. Per USCIS's Characteristics of H-1B Workers, FY2025 Report to Congress (Apr. 2026; cited at 91 FR 54821 n.14), of 406,348 approvals: 57.5% held a Master's, 8.1% a Doctorate, and 3.7% a Professional degree, so 69.3% held a graduate or professional credential. Among new hires, 1 in 7 (14.0%) is a PhD. Yet the fee applies identically to every petition (91 FR 54836). This is not a tailored user fee. It is a barrier to exactly the advanced-degree talent the program exists to admit. 3. This talent builds American companies. Many of the nation's leading firms were founded or are led by people widely reported to have begun their U.S. careers on H-1B or similar work visas: Satya Nadella (Microsoft), Sundar Pichai (Google), Eric Yuan (Zoom), Elon Musk (Tesla and SpaceX), Shantanu Narayen (Adobe), Arvind Krishna (IBM), Thomas Kurian (Google Cloud), Jyoti Bansal (AppDynamics and Harness), Jan Koum (WhatsApp), Max Levchin (PayPal), and Indra Nooyi (PepsiCo). The fee weighs most heavily on the startups and small employers that are the seedbed of such enterprise, at the front end, before any contribution can materialize. 4. And it drives American research. Foreign-born scientists are disproportionately represented among top U.S. researchers. Immigrants account for roughly 35% to 40% of U.S.-affiliated Nobel laureates in the sciences. Recent examples include Katalin Karikó (mRNA vaccine pioneer and 2023 Nobel laureate, from Hungary) and Feng Zhang (CRISPR, MIT and Broad Institute), alongside leaders shaping artificial intelligence such as Fei-Fei Li (Stanford, from China) and Yann LeCun (from France). H-1B is the standard route by which PhD graduates of U.S. universities move into U.S. industry research rather than taking that talent abroad. Taxing their entry is contrary to the national interest in scientific leadership. Statement and request. This rule would raise about $8.8 billion a year, not to adjudicate the petitions it taxes, but to fund functions across six agencies unrelated to the people paying. DHS has quantified $8.8 billion in cost and, by its own A-4 statement, zero monetized benefit ("Not Estimated," Table 12). That is not a reasoned user fee. It is a barrier that trades away American innovation and research leadership for revenue. If more funding is needed, the remedy lies with Congress's appropriations power, not an unprecedented fee that prices specialized talent out of the United States. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed rule.

text: The Verbatim Check This image captures the visual embodiment of a forensic finding: the presence of identical language across supposedly independent news outlets. The scene is a dark, empty newsroom at midnight. Rows of desks stretch into the distance, each with a computer monitor still glowing. On every single screen, the exact same headline is visible: "GAS STATION HEROIN." The words appear in identical fonts, but the website banners at the top of each screen are different—local papers, national outlets, regional broadcasters. The same phrase, replicated across all of them. Papers are scattered on the floor, each one bearing the same words in the same order. The walls are covered in newspaper clippings, all repeating the same metaphor. On a single editor's desk in the foreground sits a stack of press releases. The source line is blank. The lighting is cold and blue, coming only from the screens. The repetition is the point. This is not a room where news is written. This is a room where news is received, formatted, and broadcast without question. The image is presented as part of a forensic analysis of media narratives surrounding 7-Hydroxymitragynine and kratom. The phrase "Gas Station Heroin" appears verbatim across dozens of outlets within a narrow window of time—often on the same day, often with the same surrounding sentences, often without attribution to any original source. This pattern, the analysis argues, is not organic reporting. It is the signature of a coordinated media toolkit: a phrase manufactured once, distributed widely, and repeated until it becomes accepted as fact. Key Evidence Shown in the Image: The Phrase: "Sometimes referred to collectively as 'gas station heroin,' the drugs have been restricted by several states, but they are not scheduled at the federal level." The Outlets: coloradohometownweekly.com (2025-07-29) foxnews.com (2025-07-29) bostonglobe.com (2025-07-29) thereporteronline.com (2025-07-29) nypost.com (2025-07-29) broomfieldenterprise.com (2025-07-29) usatoday.com (2025-07-30) bangordailynews.com (2025-07-29) The Finding: Independent outlets. Identical language. Same day. No original source disclosed. The Implication: When a metaphor appears simultaneously across dozens of unrelated publishers—from national networks to hyperlocal weeklies—it raises a specific question: Did these journalists all independently arrive at the same unusual phrase, or did the phrase arrive at them? The forensic analysis argues the latter. This image is the visual evidence of that argument: a newsroom where the work has already been done somewhere else, by someone else, and the only task left is repetition. Presented for educational and analytical purposes. This image is part of a broader exhibit examining patterns of media coordination, source concealment, and narrative control. Not a statement of fact about any individual outlet, but a documentation of a statistical pattern.

text: Re: Rescission of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001 The Salmon River, in the fall, draws me back again and again to watch Coho and Chinook salmon returning to their spawning grounds in the Mt. Hood National Forest. I have known this place for over 30 years, a much shorter time than the many Native American tribes that have cared for this land since time immemorial. I consider the Salmon River area a sacred space where I can go to connect with nature and be fascinated and inspired by the amazing plants and wildlife I find there. The old-growth forest here supports a healthy habitat for many important plant and animal species that are unique to this area. I am filing this comment to oppose the rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, Docket FS-2025-0001, because that rule protects exactly what I have come to value and what cannot speak for itself. Plant and animals are not given a place at the negotiating table. I am speaking for them here. The proposal argues that the 2001 rule exceeded the agency's statutory authority, but the courts that actually reviewed that question reached the opposite conclusion. The Tenth Circuit held, in language I ask be entered against this record: "Exercising jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1291, we REVERSE the district court’s order granting Plaintiffs declaratory relief and issuing a permanent injunction, and REMAND the case for the district court to vacate the permanent injunction." The agency must address that holding, explain why it believes the 2001 rule exceeded the authority Congress granted under the Organic Act and the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act, and set out on the record the full legal basis for any position that contradicts the Tenth Circuit's conclusion that the rule did not create de facto wilderness. My connection to the Salmon River is inseparable from the health of its water. It is inevitable that building new roads creates runoff and additional sediment into streams and rivers, and that sediment buries salmon spawning beds. The scientific record already confirms the mechanism: removing riparian vegetation can raise stream temperatures beyond what suits cold-water species, and warmer temperatures can reduce egg survival, rearing densities and growth of coho salmon, with the affected area including Essential Fish Habitat and critical habitats managed by NMFS (DEIS; Carter 2005). Oregon alone holds 1,522 municipal water intakes in watersheds containing affected roadless areas (DEIS Table 35), and the state contains 211 inventoried roadless areas totaling 1,937,741 acres. Rescinding the rule in that landscape is not an abstraction. What analysis has the agency conducted of sediment and thermal loading to salmon spawning habitat specifically within the roadless areas of Mt. Hood National Forest, and what does that analysis show? The agency's own document acknowledges that habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75 percent, yet no projection of that range across the 40.1 million acres of potentially affected environment appears anywhere in the record. A finding of that magnitude, applied to the old-growth forest community I have spent three decades returning to, cannot be cited and then set aside. The agency must apply that cited fragmentation range to the full extent of the potentially affected acreage before any decision is made. The DEIS also cites the finding that elk survival rates increased during a road closure and decreased when the gates were removed (Cole 1997), and that elk avoid roads and select unroaded habitat, yet nowhere does the document project what rescission means for big game populations or for the hunting opportunity that depends on them. The agency should project those effects across each alternative it considers. Finally, the agency acknowledges that these inventoried roadless areas contain about 5 percent of the stored forest carbon in the coterminous United States, roughly 0.9 billion metric tons, and concludes these lands will continue to sequester and store carbon without analyzing what harvest and roading would actually do to that figure. The Salmon River area and the broader Mt. Hood roadless landscape are part of that carbon reservoir. The agency must quantify the change in carbon storage and sequestration under each alternative before this rulemaking proceeds. The management of our public lands should always take into consideration how actions will affect the important wildlife habitat. I urge the agency to withdraw the proposed rescission. Sincerely, Carole Miles Gresham, Oregon

text: Acting Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination, USDA Forest Service Joshua White,Dear Joshua White, USDA Forest Service Acting Director of Ecosystem Management Coordination, and Members of Congress:I'm respectfully writing to oppose the US Forest Service's proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule). Roads not only endanger the land, it's detrimentally impacts the wildlife who rely on those gateways.For a quarter century, the Roadless Rule has provided an essential layer of protection for approximately 58.5 million-acres of National Forest System lands, or about a third of all lands managed by the USDA Forest Service (Forest Service). “Inventoried Roadless Areas” (IRAs) protected by the Roadless Rule represent many of the wildest, healthiest, and most intact landscapes in the United States (https://www.pfpi.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Roadless-Rule-Rescision-Threatens-Preprint-Mildrexler-et-al.-2026.pdf). The famous Long Trail and Appalachian Trail traverse numerous Inventoried Roadless Areas protected by the Roadless Rule. Equally important, the Roadless Rule safeguards clean drinking water, protects against floods and droughts, and supports the region's native biodiversity, including imperiled species like the Northern Long-eared Bat, brook trout, Canada lynx, Bicknell's Thrush, and American marten, among many others.Only 3.3% of New England is protected from timber harvest and road construction, but scientists say we must protect at least 10% of the region for the benefit of biodiversity, carbon storage, and the wellbeing of our communities. Most fires are started by people, and a recent study found that fires are four times more likely to start near roads (https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-026-00450-2). The Roadless Rule also protects culturally-important sites and subsistence use areas. These spaces are critical to food security for many indigenous communities as well as for sustaining cultural and spiritual practices, including hunting, fishing, and gathering forest plants for food, medicine, and traditional arts.Please drop this plan to rescind the Roadless Rule or select Alternative 1, No Action.Finally, I am calling on my members of Congress to co-sponsor and pass the Roadless Area Conservation Act of 2025, H.R.3930 and S.2042, to codify the Roadless Rule in statute.Thank you.GerianneNew Hampshire

text: I submit this formal public comment in opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), Fee for Certain H–1B Petitions (Docket ID: USCIS-2026-0298). The NPRM proposes an unprecedented $103,265 supplemental fee on cap-subject H–1B petitions at filing. While framed as a multi-agency cost-recovery mechanism, this regulatory action suffers from severe statutory, procedural, and economic defects under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 500 et seq., and the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). DHS should withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety. I. Statutory Ultra Vires: The Proposed Fee Violates INA § 286(m) The proposed fee exceeds statutory authority under Section 286(m) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m). Congress authorized fee collection to recover the "full costs of providing such services"—specifically, the direct and indirect costs of processing and adjudicating petitions. Converting an H–1B adjudication into a broad revenue engine to fund general administrative and enforcement operations across disparate cabinet agencies (DHS, DOJ, DOS, and DOL) transforms a lawful user fee into an unauthorized tax. Leveraging a single employment visa category to subsidize unrelated federal operations exceeds any reasonable interpretation of INA § 286(m). An agency possesses only those powers delegated by Congress; imposing a six-figure levy without explicit statutory authority renders the rule ultra vires. II. Arbitrary and Capricious Rulemaking Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A) Under the APA, agency action must be set aside if it is arbitrary, capricious, or an abuse of discretion. An agency acts arbitrarily when it fails to articulate a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)). 1. Lack of Cost Accounting: The docket fails to present an auditable cost-study linking $103,265 to actual adjudicative expenditures attributable to H–1B filings. Disconnected from actual service delivery, the sum appears punitive and arbitrary. 2. Non-Compliance with OMB Circular A-25: User charges must reflect the direct and indirect cost to the government of providing a special benefit. Exceeding actual processing costs by orders of magnitude conflicts with established federal user-fee standards. III. Failure to Satisfy the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. § 601 et seq.) The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) requires agencies to assess impacts on small entities and evaluate less burdensome alternatives. 1. Disproportionate Impact on SMEs: A fixed $103,265 fee per employee creates an insurmountable entry barrier for small businesses, technology startups, and specialized research entities, effectively pricing them out of the cap-subject lottery while large, well-capitalized corporations absorb the overhead. 2. Omission of Meaningful Alternatives: DHS failed to adequately analyze tiered fee structures based on employer size, revenue, or wage levels, or to consider phased implementations, violating RFA procedural mandates (5 U.S.C. § 603). IV. Economic Distortion and Offshoring Incentives Exorbitant upfront fees misalign with national workforce goals by placing domestic employers at a extreme cost disadvantage. Rather than expanding domestic opportunity, the rule incentivizes companies to offshore critical research, software engineering, and technical development to overseas jurisdictions. Conclusion The proposed $103,265 fee under Docket ID USCIS-2026-0298 exceeds statutory authority under INA § 286(m), fails the reasoned decision-making standard of the APA, and causes unanalyzed economic harm to small businesses. DHS should immediately withdraw this rulemaking and align any future fee proposals strictly with audited adjudicative costs as required by law

text: To: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security From: An Concerned Individual / Industry Professional Date: September 1, 2026 Subject: Response to Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions Docket No.: ⁠USCIS-2026-0298⁠ | RIN: 1615-AD20 I. Introduction & Position Statement I am submitting formal comments in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding the $103,265 fee on cap-subject H-1B petitions. While intended to generate ~$8.8 billion annually for federal operations, this regulation exceeds statutory user-fee authority, inflicts severe economic damage, harms U.S. higher education enrollment, and actively drives high-paying technical jobs to foreign offshore delivery centers. II. Statutory Overreach Under the Immigration & Nationality Act (INA) Under 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m) (INA § 286(m)), fee collection authority granted to DHS/USCIS is strictly bounded by direct cost recovery for adjudicating benefits. Imposing a $103,265 fee per filing to generate revenue for unrelated interagency functions—including immigration courts, law enforcement, and multi-agency operations—crosses the legal threshold from an administrative user fee into an unauthorized tax. Federal courts have repeatedly held that fee-setting authority cannot be used as an unauthorized tax absent explicit Congressional authorization. III. Severe Impact on Higher Education & International Student Enrollment The proposed rule creates critical downstream harms for American colleges and universities: 1. Destruction of Post-Graduation Career Pathways: International students invest heavily in U.S. higher education largely due to post-graduation work authorization (OPT) and subsequent H-1B sponsorship. Applying this fee to inside-the-U.S. change-of-status petitions effectively forces employers to stop sponsoring recent international graduates to avoid the mandatory $103,265 penalty. 2. Decline in University Enrollment: Without a viable pathway to U.S. employment, prospective international students will choose universities in countries offering clear work pathways (e.g., Canada, the UK, Australia, Germany). 3. Multi-Billion-Dollar Loss in Tuition Revenue: International students pay full, non-subsidized tuition that directly funds university operations, domestic student programs, and research labs. A drop in international enrollment will inflict severe financial losses across U.S. higher education. IV. Acceleration of Technical Job Offshoring Imposing a non-refundable $103,265 penalty per filing will not force companies to fill specialized technical roles domestically when critical skill shortages exist. Instead, it creates a direct cost incentive to transfer technical work abroad: 1. Extreme Cost Distortion: For the total upfront cost of sponsoring one U.S.-based specialized engineer (salary + legal costs + $103,265 regulatory fee), an employer can recruit, onboard, and maintain a team of three to five senior engineers in overseas technical hubs. 2. Expansion of Global Capability Centers (GCCs): U.S. enterprises will respond by expanding Global Capability Centers (GCCs) in technology hubs across Asia (e.g., India, Philippines, Vietnam) and Europe. Rather than outsourcing secondary tasks, companies will move core end-to-end engineering—including cloud architecture and software development—to foreign delivery centers. 3. Permanent Loss of U.S. Economic Benefits: When specialized roles shift offshore, the U.S. economy suffers a permanent net loss in federal, state, and local income taxes, alongside real estate and consumer spending. V. Harm to Startups and Small Businesses While multinational corporations have foreign subsidiaries to reallocate work, small-to-medium enterprises (SMEs) and high-growth domestic startups do not. Small businesses requiring specialized technical talent cannot afford a $103,265 fee per candidate, putting domestic innovators at a severe competitive disadvantage relative to foreign firms and massive conglomerates. VI. Conclusion The proposed $103,265 fee is legally flawed under the APA, economically counterproductive, damages international student enrollment, and incentivizes the offshoring of key technical positions. DHS should withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. Respectfully submitted, An Concerned Individual / Industry Professional

text: Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed repeal of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule. I am a young person living in Colorado, who enjoys spending time in outdoor spaces. It is important to protect and conserve these spaces to ensure that species that rely on areas away from developed spaces have a place to exist. Roadless areas support diverse and abundant wildlife and plant communities. Human activities, primarily road construction, are by far the most extensive agents of forest fragmentation in the United States. Fragmentation is considered one of the leading causes of native species loss and the present extinction crisis (Heilman et al., 2002). The USDA highlighted an experimental study in a roadless area of southern Idaho that found road noise alone caused more than a quarter decline in bird abundance, with nearly a third of species avoiding the noise entirely (USDA Forest Service, 2026). Nearly one-fifth of roadless area watersheds rank in the top quartile for aquatic biodiversity within their states, supporting rich native aquatic fauna (Olden et al., 2026). Repealing the Roadless Rule threatens the intact habitat that supports this abundance and diversity of species. Roadless areas are essential habitats for many federally threatened and endangered species. A biological assessment in the Forest Service's Draft Environmental Impact Statement made a "may affect, likely to adversely affect" determination for 327 ESA-listed species and 71 designated critical habitats under the proposed repeal (USDA Forest Service, 2026). Roadless Areas contain more than 220 threatened or endangered species, representing roughly 25% of all listed or proposed animal species and 13% of listed plant species in the United States (Loucks et al., 2003). text: Dear Affirmative Asylum Referrals Without Interview, Docket ID: USCIS-2026-0199 I am writing to oppose the interim final rule allowing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to refer affirmative asylum applications to immigration court without an interview. The asylum interview is not a formality. For many people, it is the first and only chance to explain in a non-adversarial setting, to a trained officer why they fled their home country and why they fear returning. This rule allows that opportunity to be skipped entirely, and lets USCIS refer someone into removal proceedings based on a paper record alone. The rule text admits this policy will send applications they could have approved to immigration court, where asylum seekers have no right to government-appointed counsel and where immigration judges are making decisions in increasingly adversarial settings. It also removes the requirement that an officer explain whether they found the applicant credible when making that decision. I am especially concerned that this rule will affect people who missed a filing deadline, who have limited English or legal support, or whose written applications don't fully capture what happened to them — people who might otherwise have been able to explain themselves in an interview. These policies will disproportionately affect the most vulnerable asylum seekers and continue to increase pressure on already-overwhelmed immigration courts. The right to due process ensures that every person can meaningfully take part in their own case, and this policy removes a critical guardrail against asylum seekers' applications being unjustly adjudicated. It makes it more likely that people with real, valid claims for protection will be sent into deportation proceedings without ever being heard. I urge USCIS to withdraw this rule and restore the right to an interview for every asylum applicant. Thank you Emily Shapiro Bronx, NY Sincerely, Ms. Emily Shapiro

title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
note: US government record, public domain. A public comment filed on a federal rulemaking: prose written to change an outcome, which is the register these lenses were authored for and neither the Federal Register nor congressional hearings supplied.
text: I respectfully oppose the proposed $103,265 fee for certain cap-subject H-1B petitions. I understand and support the goal of protecting American workers, preventing abuse of the H-1B program, and making sure employers pay fair wages. However, a blanket fee of more than $100,000 per petition is not a targeted way to achieve those goals. In practice, it could hurt U.S. businesses, especially startups and smaller employers, while encouraging companies to move skilled jobs and projects outside the United States. One of the biggest concerns is that this fee would affect small and large employers very differently. A multinational company may be able to absorb a $103,265 fee or move the employee to an overseas office. A startup, small engineering firm, hospital, research organization, or growing technology company may simply be unable to afford it. DHS's own analysis estimates that the rule could have a significant economic impact on thousands of small entities. This could unintentionally give the largest corporations an even greater advantage while making it harder for smaller American companies to compete. The proposal also appears to assume that if an employer does not hire an H-1B worker, the company will hire a U.S. worker instead. That will not always happen. Many technology, engineering, financial, scientific, and other professional jobs can now be performed from other countries. If it becomes too expensive to employ a skilled worker in the United States, companies may move the position or an entire project to Canada, India, Europe, Mexico, or another country. In that situation, the United States does not gain an American job. It loses the job altogether. The U.S. can also lose the payroll taxes, income taxes, consumer spending, technical knowledge, innovation, and additional jobs supported by that worker and the work being performed here. Research has shown that highly skilled immigration can contribute to innovation, productivity, and economic activity in the United States. H-1B workers are employed in areas such as technology, engineering, medicine, research, finance, and other specialized fields where their work often supports larger teams that include American workers. For this reason, the economic impact of this rule should not be measured only by how much money the government collects in fees. DHS estimates that the proposal could collect billions of dollars annually. But fee revenue is not the same as a net economic benefit. The government should also consider the value of work that may move overseas, businesses that may decide not to expand in the United States, lost tax revenue, reduced investment, and the effect on American innovation and competitiveness. I am also concerned that the proposed fee does not appear reasonably connected to the actual cost of processing one H-1B petition. Employers would effectively be asked to pay more than $100,000 for a petition partly to fund broader government activities. That is an extraordinary financial burden to place on a relatively small group of employers. The fee also does little to distinguish between legitimate employers and companies that may be abusing the program. A company with enough money can still pay the fee. A legitimate small employer may not be able to. If the goal is to prevent abuse or protect U.S. wages, there are better approaches. DHS could strengthen prevailing-wage requirements, increase enforcement against fraudulent employers, conduct more audits, improve transparency, impose stronger penalties for violations, or place additional requirements on employers that use unusually large numbers of H-1B workers. Those policies would address the actual problem more directly. The United States is also competing with other countries for skilled workers. Canada and other nations are actively trying to attract engineers, scientists, technology professionals, medical professionals, researchers, and entrepreneurs. Making it more than $100,000 more expensive to employ a skilled worker in the United States gives businesses another reason to locate high-value work elsewhere. The goal should be to keep innovation, investment, skilled jobs, and growing companies in the United States. I therefore ask DHS not to finalize the proposed $103,265 fee. If additional H-1B fees are necessary, DHS should consider a much more reasonable fee structure that takes employer size into account, protects small businesses and startups, targets actual abuse, and reflects the real administrative cost of the program. Protecting American workers and allowing American businesses to hire highly skilled people are not conflicting goals. A well-designed H-1B program can do both. This proposal, however, risks raising government revenue at the cost of American businesses, innovation, investment, tax revenue, and jobs that could ultimately move outside the United States.

title: Comment from Steven Singleton

text: Harmonizing anomaly response into one three-tier structure across gas (49 CFR Part 192) and hazardous liquid (Part 195) is a real improvement: operators running both, and inspectors auditing both, currently work from two vocabularies for the same engineering question. Moving away from dent-depth-alone criteria toward interacting-threat evaluation also reflects that depth by itself predicts failure poorly. The structural reform is worth finalizing. The comments below go to how several terms within it are drawn. NEAR-TERM DEADLINES OUTSIDE HIGH-CONSEQUENCE AREAS The proposal sets near-term response at one year inside HCAs and two years elsewhere. Under 49 U.S.C. 60109, Congress directed the Secretary to prescribe standards identifying pipelines in high-density population and environmentally sensitive areas. That framework marks where consequences are gravest; it does not establish that consequences elsewhere are slight. A characterized defect outside a mapped HCA still sits near someone's home, water source, or land. Two requests. First, PHMSA should state on the record how the proposed near-term deadlines compare to the deadlines they replace, and quantify any net change in time-at-risk — the preamble should not leave the public to infer whether urgency has increased or decreased. Second, the agency should justify two years specifically for a defect already identified and characterized as warranting response. The agency has revisited this subject recently, including the repair-criteria corrections at 90 FR 3713 (Jan. 15, 2025), and a clear statement now would settle the question rather than defer it. CHOICE OF ANALYSIS METHOD The rule lists several permitted models for metal-loss and crack analysis and allows "other models demonstrated to provide comparable results," with toughness from "Charpy v-notch or other valid testing methods." The referenced standards are the rule's own; the difficulty is that "comparable" and "valid" are undefined while the operator both selects the method and lives with the result. That is not an accusation of bad faith — it is an auditability gap, since an inspector reviewing the file afterward has no record of what was chosen or why. Fix: define the comparability standard, and require the operator to record the method selected and the basis for selecting it. Engineering teams document this internally already, so the added burden is small. "SUBJECT MATTER EXPERT" Anomaly evaluation must be performed by a subject matter expert, but the proposal does not state qualifications or address independence. PHMSA should set a minimum qualification and say whether the expert may be an employee of the operator whose repair schedule is under evaluation. TEMPORARY PRESSURE REDUCTION Pressure reduction is permitted pending permanent repair, and PHMSA should confirm whether any outer limit bounds how long a segment may operate that way. If none is specified, "temporary" carries no content, and a measure meant as a bridge could become the steady state. Setting a maximum duration, or requiring a dated repair schedule when the reduction begins, would resolve it. THE 180-DAY DISCOVERY WINDOW Discovery runs from the operator "having adequate information," a condition largely within the operator's control. Tying the trigger to a dated, retained record — receipt of tool-run results, or written notice of the anomaly — would anchor the window to something verifiable after the fact. NOTICE TO THOSE BEARING THE RESIDUAL RISK Residents along rights-of-way, local emergency responders, tribal governments, and drinking-water utilities are not parties here, yet they carry the risk during any deferral. Will PHMSA require notice to local emergency responders when a defect is identified and repair is deferred beyond one year? Responders who know a segment's condition can stage resources accordingly. Harmonization deserves to go forward. Defining the terms above would let it do so on a record that an inspector, and a resident, can both check.

text: Acting Director, Ecosystem Management Coordination, USDA Forest Service Joshua White,Dear Joshua White, USDA Forest Service Acting Director of Ecosystem Management Coordination, and Members of Congress:I'm respectfully writing to oppose the US Forest Service's proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule (Roadless Rule). Please drop this plan or select Alternative 1, No Action.As someone who works extensively in the outdoor recreation sector as a consultant and market researcher, protecting these lands is in our best interest both economically and for our overall public health. I have measured the impact of access to these places, and it is far-reaching and relevant. For a quarter century, the Roadless Rule has provided an essential layer of protection for approximately 58.5 million-acres of National Forest System lands, or about a third of all lands managed by the USDA Forest Service (Forest Service). “Inventoried Roadless Areas” (IRAs) protected by the Roadless Rule represent many of the wildest, healthiest, and most intact landscapes in the United States (https://www.pfpi.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Roadless-Rule-Rescision-Threatens-Preprint-Mildrexler-et-al.-2026.pdf). Over 1.5 million Americans submitted comments in support of the Roadless Rule when it was developed, a record for public participation in federal rulemaking that still holds to this day.In New England, the Roadless Rule protects 260,000 acres, or approximately one-fifth of the White and Green Mountain National Forests, combined. Iconic landscapes protected by the Rule include places like New Hampshire’s Franconia Notch, Mt Moosilauke, Mt Chocorua, and the Presidential Range, as well as Vermont’s White Rocks. The famous Long Trail and Appalachian Trail traverse numerous Inventoried Roadless Areas protected by the Roadless Rule. Equally important, the Roadless Rule safeguards clean drinking water, protects against floods and droughts, and supports the region's native biodiversity, including imperiled species like the Northern Long-eared Bat, brook trout, Canada lynx, Bicknell's Thrush, and American marten, among many others.Only 3.3% of New England is protected from timber harvest and road construction, but scientists say we must protect at least 10% of the region for the benefit of biodiversity, carbon storage, and the wellbeing of our communities. Rescinding the Roadless Rule would set our region back in time, making New England's conservation goals even harder to achieve.Recognizing the exceptional value of Inventoried Roadless Areas (totaling just 2% of the lower-48 states), as well as the Forest Service’s unsustainable multi-billion dollar road maintenance backlog, the agency promulgated the Roadless Rule as “a down payment on the well-being of future generations,” in the words of former Forest Service Chief Mike Dombeck, who oversaw the Rule’s development.A recent study found that in New England, the Roadless Rule helps to protect drinking water for 8.8% of Vermont residents and 7.3% of New Hampshire residents (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pwat.0000538). Additionally, 7% of Massachusetts residents get their water from sources that originate in Inventoried Roadless Areas in the White Mountain National Forest.Importantly, the Roadless Rule is also among our best tools for addressing wildfire. Most fires are started by people, and a recent study found that fires are four times more likely to start near roads (https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-026-00450-2). The Roadless Rule also protects culturally-important sites and subsistence use areas. These spaces are critical to food security for many indigenous communities as well as for sustaining cultural and spiritual practices, including hunting, fishing, and gathering forest plants for food, medicine, and traditional arts.Please drop this plan to rescind the Roadless Rule or select Alternative 1, No Action.Finally, I am calling on my members of Congress to co-sponsor and pass the Roadless Area Conservation Act of 2025, H.R.3930 and S.2042, to codify the Roadless Rule in statute.Thank you.ScottMaine

text: The proposed $103,265 fee stretches INA § 286(m) beyond what Congress authorized. That statute allows DHS to set user fees to recover the reasonable administrative cost of providing adjudication services. Processing an I-129 petition does not cost anywhere near six figures; instead, the agency arrived at this number by bundling roughly $8.8 billion in interagency operating and enforcement expenses and dumping it across 85,000 cap petitions. When an agency charges an amount that bears no rational relationship to the service provided and uses the proceeds to fund general government functions, it ceases to be an administrative user fee and becomes a tax—a power that belongs exclusively to Congress. text: Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed repeal of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule. As a student at UC Berkeley originally from out of state, something that drew me to California was its abundance of diverse natural beauty. Maintaining this beauty through a more hands off approach is really important to me as someone who finds serenity in the untouched. Roadless areas support local businesses through recreational use. They protect more than 11,000 climbing and bouldering routes, over 1,000 whitewater paddling runs, and more than 70,000 kilometers of trails, which were estimated in 2017 to have a value of over $500 million (Olden et al., 2026). The Forest Service has identified in their own Draft Environmental Impact Statement (2026) that the proposed rescission would result in local economic losses equal to $9 million per year from reduced trail-based, dispersed, and wildlife-related recreation. That figure uses the agency's conservative assumption of just a 1% loss in visits (USDA Forest Service, 2026). Roadless areas support diverse and abundant wildlife and plant communities. Human activities, primarily road construction, are by far the most extensive agents of forest fragmentation in the United States. Fragmentation is considered one of the leading causes of native species loss and the present extinction crisis (Heilman et al., 2002). The USDA highlighted an experimental study in a roadless area of southern Idaho that found road noise alone caused more than a quarter decline in bird abundance, with nearly a third of species avoiding the noise entirely (USDA Forest Service, 2026). Nearly one-fifth of roadless area watersheds rank in the top quartile for aquatic biodiversity within their states, supporting rich native aquatic fauna (Olden et al., 2026). Repealing the Roadless Rule threatens the intact habitat that supports this abundance and diversity of species. By supporting the roadless rule, the USDA would help maintain and protect diverse wildlife and plant communities while also giving people a space for outdoor recreation. text: Dear Director, I have significant concerns about the Notice of Intent to revise the U.S. Forest Service Travel Management Rule. Changing the Forest Services approach to motorized access from closed unless designated open to open unless designated closed would set the Forest Service back 20 years in its efforts to sustainably manage recreation, protect natural resources, and provide healthy wildlife habitat. The Forest Service has previously attempted to manage motor vehicle access under this paradigm and experience has shown that it results in unsustainable natural resource impacts, brings serious public safety concerns, and increases conflict. All national forest visitors should have access to safe, enjoyable, recreation opportunities. All travel management decisions - including decisions regarding where e-bikes are appropriate - should continue to be made locally and not dictated by a top-down D.C. policy. I request that you not change the current Travel Management Rule. Travel management impacts everybody who visits a national forest or grassland. Any changes to the Travel Management Rule must seek to balance motor vehicle access with the Forest Services resource protection responsibilities, public safety considerations, and the interests of all national forest users. Sincerely, Anne Lirette

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16965
note: US government record, public domain. A public comment filed on a federal rulemaking: prose written to change an outcome, which is the register these lenses were authored for and neither the Federal Register nor congressional hearings supplied.
text: I strongly and unequivocally oppose the proposed rescission of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This proposal should be withdrawn in its entirety. The Roadless Rule protects approximately 44.7 million acres of National Forest System land from most new road construction, road reconstruction, and commercial timber harvesting. These lands are among America’s remaining intact forests and watersheds. They provide clean drinking water, wildlife habitat, fisheries, recreation, carbon storage, and functioning ecosystems that cannot simply be recreated once they are fragmented by roads and development. The administration’s argument that rescinding the Roadless Rule is necessary to reduce wildfire risk is not convincing. The rule does not prohibit all forest-health or wildfire-management activities. If protecting communities from wildfire is the objective, resources should be directed toward prescribed fire, defensible space, targeted fuels reduction, and other measures that directly protect people and communities. Building roads into remote forests is not a substitute for those measures. In fact, roads can increase human access, habitat fragmentation, erosion, invasive species, and opportunities for human-caused wildfire ignition. Research cited in recent reporting has found lower wildfire density in protected forests and greater wildfire occurrence in areas associated with roads and human activity. Removing roadless protections therefore risks making some forests more vulnerable to the very problem the administration claims this proposal will address. The wildlife consequences are unacceptable. A recent analysis found that rescinding the Roadless Rule could increase threats to more than 400 threatened and endangered species and put approximately 7.4 million acres of designated critical habitat and nearly 1,800 miles of protected rivers and streams at risk. Habitat fragmentation is a well-established driver of population decline and extinction risk. The federal government should not deliberately remove protections from critical habitat for species that are already struggling to survive. The proposal also threatens people. Roadless watersheds provide essential clean water, support fisheries, recreation, tourism, and local economies, and protect downstream communities. These are tangible public benefits. They are not obstacles to responsible land management. The argument that these decisions should simply be returned to local forest managers is equally flawed. Local management decisions are subject to changing political and economic pressures. A nationwide conservation standard exists precisely to ensure that short-term interests do not permanently compromise resources belonging to all Americans. Most importantly, no presidential administration, regardless of political party, should have the authority to strip millions of acres of public land of longstanding conservation protections simply because a new administration has different political priorities. Public lands belong to the American people, not to whichever administration happens to control the executive branch. Conservation protections should not be treated as temporary political policies that can be dismantled and rebuilt every four or eight years. If anything, we should be moving in the opposite direction. We need more protected roadless forests, not fewer. We need more intact watersheds, not more roads through them. We need stronger protections for wildlife habitat, not weaker ones. And we need to preserve the remaining places where ecosystems can function with minimal human disturbance. Once roads fragment an intact landscape, the resulting ecological damage can be permanent or extremely difficult to reverse. Once critical habitat is degraded and species populations collapse, simply changing management policy later cannot guarantee recovery. I therefore urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the U.S. Forest Service to reject this proposal and retain the Roadless Area Conservation Rule in full. I further urge the Forest Service to pursue policies that expand and strengthen protections for America’s remaining roadless and ecologically intact public lands. The federal government should leave future generations with more intact forests, cleaner water, healthier wildlife populations, and protected public lands than we inherited. I vehemently oppose rescinding the Roadless Rule. This proposal moves federal land management in exactly the wrong direction and should be withdrawn.
